story.headline: Car bomb hits Colombia after new president
story.summary: A car bomb struck a Cauca highway toll plaza a day after right-wing newcomer Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia's president.
story.display_body: A car bomb exploded at a highway toll plaza in Colombia's southwestern Cauca department on Saturday 8 August 2026, one day after right-wing political newcomer Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as president. The device detonated at a toll station on the Pan-American Highway — the main road artery of Colombia's southwest — wounding two security guards; no deaths were reported. The army attributed the attack to two dissident factions of the former FARC (Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, the guerrilla army that demobilised under a 2016 peace accord), splinter groups that rejected that deal and remain active in Cauca. De la Espriella, a lawyer who campaigned on a hard-line security platform, took office in Cali on Friday 7 August, succeeding the leftist Gustavo Petro. "Colombia will not kneel before violence, nor will it allow the destruction of the infrastructure that connects our regions," Transport Minister Elsa Noguera said.
story.why: the bombing is an immediate security test for a president elected on promises of a tougher line against armed groups, and it signals the dissidents' capacity to strike national infrastructure at the very start of his term.

story.headline: Iran sets conditions to reopen Hormuz
story.summary: Iran's Supreme National Security Council set six conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz as President Pezeshkian urged a deal with the US.
story.display_body: Iran's Supreme National Security Council set six conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, its secretary said in remarks reported Saturday 8 August 2026, a day before President Masoud Pezeshkian said "now is the best time" for a deal with the United States. The strait — the narrow chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil passes — has been shut to commercial shipping amid the Iran–US confrontation that opened earlier in 2026. Council secretary Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr said it would reopen only once Washington ends threats and what he called "insults" to Iran, permanently halts attacks on Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq, lifts what he termed a US naval blockade and pulls its forces back from the region, pays compensation for two "imposed wars", lifts sanctions, and releases frozen Iranian assets. "The Supreme National Security Council will never back down, neither in war nor in negotiations," he said. Pezeshkian, on Sunday 9 August, struck a more conciliatory note, saying Iran should move beyond a state of "neither war nor peace" and needed a dispute-resolution mechanism rather than a return to fighting.
story.why: the list formalises and broadens Iran's terms — explicitly extending its red lines to Yemen and Iraq — and the daylight between the council's maximalism and the president's opening reflects the internal split that will shape whether the standoff eases or hardens.

story.headline: Israel tenders 627 West Bank settler homes
story.summary: Israel's Land Authority published a tender for 627 settler homes at Kochav Yaakov on occupied West Bank land near Ramallah.
story.display_body: Israel's Land Authority published a tender on Wednesday 6 August 2026 for 627 settler homes at Kochav Yaakov, an existing settlement north of Jerusalem built on land of the occupied West Bank's Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate. The tender, numbered 177/2026, sets 30 November 2026 as the deadline for construction firms to bid and covers about 253 dunums (roughly 25 hectares); the project was approved in April 2025, so the release marks its move from planning to construction. Palestinian monitors at the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission — a body that tracks Israeli settlement activity — recorded 12 such tenders in the first half of 2026, covering 1,138 units across five settlement blocs. Settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.
story.why: continued tendering entrenches Israeli construction on occupied land around Ramallah even as a fragile Gaza ceasefire is being renegotiated, narrowing the territorial basis for any future Palestinian state.

story.headline: Swiss minister urges spiking protections
story.summary: Health Minister Baume-Schneider called for better protection against chemical submission after an Aargau drink-spiking abuse case.
story.display_body: Federal Councillor Elisabeth Baume-Schneider, the health minister, called on Sunday 9 August 2026 for stronger protection against "chemical submission" — sedating a victim with drugs in order to assault them — after a high-profile Aargau case. In an interview with SonntagsBlick, Baume-Schneider (who heads the Federal Department of Home Affairs) said prevention and public information must improve, noting that awareness had been low that spiking assaults also happen in the home rather than only in nightlife settings, and predicting more cases will come to light. Her remarks follow the case of a former SVP cantonal MP from Untersiggenthal, in canton Aargau, arrested nearly three years ago and accused of using knockout drops to sedate and sexually abuse two women and a girl. A national strategy against domestic and gender-based violence is due to launch in 2026.
story.why: it signals a federal-level policy response — not just a cantonal prosecution — to a form of sexual violence that Swiss authorities concede is under-recognised and probably under-reported.

story.headline: Swiss towns ration water in drought
story.summary: At least 151 Swiss municipalities imposed water-use restrictions this summer, some with fines up to 2,000 francs, amid a dry year and heatwave.
story.display_body: At least 151 Swiss municipalities have imposed water-use restrictions this summer, some carrying fines of up to 2,000 francs, as a dry year and the current heatwave strain local supplies. A swissinfo.ch tally republished by SRF on Sunday 9 August 2026 found that more than 194 municipalities — mostly villages and small towns — have urged residents to save water, and that as of a 24 July count at least 151 had gone further and banned specific uses such as watering gardens, filling swimming pools and washing cars. The picture is strikingly local for a country often called "Europe's water tower": Switzerland is not running short of water overall, but supply is unevenly distributed, so some communes fear scarcity while neighbours have none. The first such orders this summer reached five villages in canton Fribourg on 22 June.
story.why: it is a concrete, enforceable constraint on daily life in the affected communes, and a sign that Alpine water abundance no longer guarantees local supply in a hot, dry summer.

story.headline: Jaccoud runs for Vaud government
story.summary: Socialist national councillor Jessica Jaccoud announced a candidacy for the Vaud cantonal government; the PS ticket is decided 26 September.
story.display_body: Socialist national councillor Jessica Jaccoud announced her candidacy for the Vaud cantonal government on Sunday 9 August 2026, as jockeying opens over the next Conseil d'État race. Jaccoud is seeking a place on the Socialist Party (PS) ticket for the executive of Vaud, Switzerland's third-most-populous canton; Lausanne's Samuel Bendahan and Yverdon's Brena Tuosto could also enter, and a party congress on 26 September 2026 will decide which candidate joins Roger Nordmann on the PS slate. The manoeuvring marks the start of an internal contest to shape who governs the French-speaking canton.
